source_text: L’habit ne fait pas le moine
english_translation: The vestment does not make the monk
Cultural_Context: Just because a monk is wearing a renunciate’s robe, it doesn’t mean that the monk is sincere in his intentions. The phrase implies that appearances can sometimes mislead one’s better judgment. The English equivalent would be, “Don’t judge a book by its cover.”

source_text: Qui vivra verra
english_translation: He/she who lives, shall see.
Cultural_Context: Something is unknown now, but will become clear in the future; the only way to find out is to wait and see. Typically used when an outcome is unpredictable or uncertain, like in the English phrase, “The future will tell.”

source_text: Chacun voit midi à sa porte
english_translation: Each person sees noon at his/her door.
Cultural_Context: Each person prioritizes their own interests, and their unique perspective on life guides how they interact with others, set goals, work and live. This saying can also refer to a person’s selfishness...

source_text: Mieux vaut prévenir que guérir
english_translation: It’s better to prevent than to heal.
Cultural_Context: It’s better to take the necessary precautions to prevent a sickness, than to have to treat and heal this sickness.

source_text: Qui n’avance pas, recule
english_translation: Who does not move forward, recedes.
Cultural_Context: There can be no standstill in life, only evolution or devolution. You can either adapt, or become stagnant and “recede.”

source_text: Il ne faut pas se fier aux apparences
english_translation: One should not trust appearances.
Cultural_Context: This saying is the English equivalent of “You can’t judge a book by its cover,” or “Looks can be deceiving.”

source_text: Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid
english_translation: Little by little, the bird makes its nest.
Cultural_Context: This proverb designates patience and perseverance. It can be used in many situations, particularly to refer to something substantial that has not yet been accomplished, but will be with time and perseverance.

source_text: Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait
english_translation: As soon as said, as soon as done.
Cultural_Context: The equivalent English saying is, “It’s as good as done.” It indicates that something is or will be done almost immediately upon request.

source_text: Bien mal acquis ne profite jamais
english_translation: A badly acquired good never benefits.
Cultural_Context: In English, the saying goes, “Ill-gotten goods seldom prosper,” or “Crime doesn’t pay,” meaning it’s best to be honest because dishonesty doesn’t get you anywhere.

source_text: Qui court deux lièvres à la fois, n’en prend aucun
english_translation: Who runs after two hares at the same time, catches none.
Cultural_Context: We ought to concentrate on one task at a time with optimal attention...

source_text: Mangez bien, riez souvent, aimez beaucoup
english_translation: Eat well, laugh often, love abundantly.
Cultural_Context: This saying is analogous to “Live life to the fullest” or carpe diem...

source_text: À jeune chasseur, il faut un vieux chien
english_translation: For the young hunter, an old dog is needed.
Cultural_Context: An inexperienced person needs someone older and wiser to show him/her the ropes.

source_text: Après la pluie, le beau temps
english_translation: After the rain, good weather.
Cultural_Context: This saying is a poetic way of saying “Hang in there.” Even if things are bad at the moment, they’ll get better.

source_text: Quand on a pas ce que l’on aime, il faut aimer ce que l’on a
english_translation: When one doesn’t have the things that one loves, one must love what one has.
Cultural_Context: It reflects the saying, “Want what you have and you’ll have what you want,”...

source_text: Bien faire et laisser dire
english_translation: Do well and let (them) speak.
Cultural_Context: Do what you believe is right and don’t pay attention to what others have to say about it.

source_text: Il n’y a pas plus sourd que celui qui ne veut pas entendre
english_translation: No one is as deaf as the one who does not want to listen.
Cultural_Context: People who are too stubborn... pay no attention to others’ advice or opinions.

source_text: Passer comme une lettre à la poste
english_translation: To go through like a letter in the mail.
Cultural_Context: ...used to refer to something... that’s easy, runs smoothly and is hassle-free.

source_text: Si jeunesse savait, si vieillesse pouvait
english_translation: If youth knew, if age could.
Cultural_Context: This saying is a French equivalent of “Youth is wasted on the young.”

source_text: Ça ne casse pas des briques
english_translation: It doesn’t break bricks.
Cultural_Context: Basically, this is the French version of “It’s nothing to write home about.”

source_text: Tiré par les cheveux
english_translation: Pulled by the hair.
Cultural_Context: This phrase means that something is “far-fetched” or unlikely.

source_text: La nuit porte conseil
english_translation: The night brings advice.
Cultural_Context: This saying is the equivalent of the English saying “Sleep on it,”...

source_text: C’est la fin des haricots
english_translation: It’s the end of the (green) beans.
Cultural_Context: ...synonymous with Il n’y a plus rien ! (“There’s nothing left!”). This saying dates back to the 18th century...

source_text: Battre le fer pendant qu’il est chaud
english_translation: Strike the iron while it’s hot.
Cultural_Context: ...means to take advantage of favorable conditions.

source_text: Il faut qu’une porte soit ouverte ou fermée
english_translation: A door must be open or closed.
Cultural_Context: Pure and simple: “You can’t have it both ways.”

source_text: Voir venir quelqu’un avec ses gros sabots
english_translation: To see someone coming with his/her big clogs.
Cultural_Context: To be able to clearly and easily decipher someone’s intentions...

source_text: Il ne faut rien laisser au hasard
english_translation: One should leave nothing to chance.
Cultural_Context: This one simply means, “Plan ahead.”

source_text: Les murs ont des oreilles
english_translation: The walls have ears.
Cultural_Context: One should pay attention to what they say, because there’s a chance they could be overheard...

source_text: Il n’y a pas de quoi fouetter un chat
english_translation: It’s nothing to whip a cat about.
Cultural_Context: It’s a lively way of saying, C’est pas grave ! (It’s no big deal!)

source_text: Tout est bien qui finit bien
english_translation: All’s well that ends well.
Cultural_Context: ...as long as the final outcomes are successful, such experiences should be considered positive overall.

source_text: Les bons comptes font les bons amis
english_translation: Good accounts make good friends.
Cultural_Context: In English we say, “A debt paid is a friend kept.”

source_text: Être sage comme une image
english_translation: To be well-behaved like a picture.
Cultural_Context: In English, an equivalent saying is “to be good as gold.”

source_text: La jeunesse est le temps d’étudier la sagesse, la vieillesse est le temps de la pratiquer
english_translation: Youth is the time to study wisdom, old age the time to practice it.
Cultural_Context: ...nothing should be taken for granted, because La vie est courte (Life is short)!

source_text: Rien ne sert de courir; il faut partir à point
english_translation: There’s no point in running; you have to set out in due time.
Cultural_Context: This one is from the first lines of “Le lièvre et la tortue”... “Slow and steady wins the race.”

source_text: Qui sème le vent, récolte la tempête
english_translation: Who sows the wind reaps the storm
Cultural_Context: ...eventually you will always have to face the consequences of your actions.

source_text: Ce n’est pas à un vieux singe qu’on apprend à faire des grimaces
english_translation: It’s not to an old monkey that one can teach to pull faces
Cultural_Context: This is a fun version of the familiar English proverb...

source_text: Il faut casser le noyau pour avoir l’amande
english_translation: You have to break the shell to get the almond
Cultural_Context: The English version of this seems much more modern...

source_text: De mauvais grain jamais bon pain
english_translation: From bad grain, never good bread
Cultural_Context: ...the quality of something depends on its origin...

source_text: Faire d'une mouche un éléphant
english_translation: Make of a fly an elephant
Cultural_Context: Another proverb that needs little explanation.

source_text: C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron
english_translation: It’s by forging that one becomes a blacksmith
Cultural_Context: This proverb transports you right back to a medieval French town...

source_text: Rome ne s'est pas faite en un jour
english_translation: Rome wasn’t made in a day
Cultural_Context: ...reminds us that great tasks take time and that we need patience...

source_text: C'est la paille et la poutre
english_translation: It's the straw and the beam
Cultural_Context: ...points out people’s ability to see faults in others while not recognising their own.

source_text: C'est vouloir prendre des lièvres au son du tambour
english_translation: It’s wanting to catch hares by beating a drum
Cultural_Context: ...refers to taking the wrong approach to doing something.

source_text: On ne fait pas boire un âne qui n'a pas soif
english_translation: You can’t make an ass drink that isn’t thirsty
Cultural_Context: ...remind us of a world where transport by horse or donkey was common.

source_text: Mieux vaut être seul que mal accompagné
english_translation: Better to be alone than in bad company
Cultural_Context: A proverb that requires little explanation.

source_text: Chien qui aboie ne mord pas
english_translation: The dog that barks doesn’t bite
Cultural_Context: Another proverb that is well known in both French and English.

source_text: à beau mentir qui vient de loiny
english_translation: long ways, long lies
Cultural_Context: (lit.: he who comes from afar can lie well; i.e.: someone from far away can more easily tell lies without fear of being caught because he is unknown in his new region)

source_text: à bon chat, bon rat
english_translation: meet one's match; tit for tat; an equal [in combat]
Cultural_Context: (lit.: a good rat for a good cat)

source_text: à bon vin, point d’enseigne
english_translation: the reputation of a good thing precedes it
Cultural_Context: (lit.: not need to explain a good wine; i.e.: what is good needs no recomendation)

source_text: à brebis tondue Dieu mesure le vent
english_translation: the Lord tempers the wind to the shorn lamb
Cultural_Context: (a Biblical reference)

source_text: à chaque jour suffit sa peine
english_translation: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for each day there suffices suffering; i.e.: deal with today’s difficulties without worrying about what might come tomorrow; n.b.: from the New Testament, Matthew 6:34)

source_text: à cheval donné on ne regarde pas le dents
english_translation: don’t look a gift horse in the mouth
Cultural_Context: (lit.: one doesn’t look at the reins of a horse given as a gift)

source_text: à cœur vaillant rien d’impossible
english_translation: nothing is impossible to a willing heart
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for a brave heart, nothing is impossible)

source_text: à l’impossible, nul n’est tenu
english_translation: no one can be expected to do the impossible
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for what is impossible, nothing is expected)

source_text: à l’œuvre on reconnaît l’artisan
english_translation: you can tell an artist by his work
Cultural_Context: (lit.: by his work one recognizes the artisan)

source_text: à la Chandeleur, l’hiver se passe ou prend vigueur
english_translation: as of February 2, winter either wanes or gains strength
Cultural_Context: (lit.: on Candlemass [Feb. 2], winter ends or becomes stronger than before; n.b.: the date Feb. 2 is also Groundhog Day, whose connotations are similar)

source_text: à la Sante-Luce, les jours croissent du saut d’une puce
english_translation: as of Sainte Luce Day (Dec. 13), the days start to lengthen ever so slowly
Cultural_Context: (lit.: on Sainte Luce, the days grow at the pace of a flea)

source_text: à mauvais ouvrier point de bons outils
english_translation: a bad workman blames his tools
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for a bad workman, no good tools)

source_text: à père avare fils prodigue
english_translation: the miser’s son is a spendthrift
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for a miserly father a prodigal son; i.e.: a vice or fault in a parent can turn into the opposite vice or fault in a child)

source_text: à quelque chose malheur est bon
english_translation: every cloud has a silver lining
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for something bad there is good; i.e.: bad things can have a positive aspect)

source_text: à tout seigneur, tout honneur
english_translation: honor to whom honor is due
Cultural_Context: (lit.: to all nobles, all honor; i.e.: honor should be bestowed upon people according to rank and achievement)

source_text: à vieille mule, frein doré
english_translation: a golden brake for an old mule
Cultural_Context: (i.e.: be nice to older animals so they can be sold at market; also used to refer to older women who apply makeup excessively)

source_text: abondance de biens ne nuit pas
english_translation: an abundance of goods does no harm
Cultural_Context: (said when receiving something that one already has in sufficient quantity)

source_text: aide-toi, le ciel t’aidera
english_translation: God helps those who help themselves
Cultural_Context: (lit.: help yourself, and the heavens will help you)

source_text: après la pluie, le beau temps
english_translation: every cloud has a silver lining; good and bad things come one after the other
Cultural_Context: (lit.: after the rain, nice weather)

source_text: araignée du matin, chagrin, araignée du soir, espoir
english_translation: seeing a spider in the morning brings bad luck, seeing a spider in the evening brings good luck
Cultural_Context: (a commonly cited French superstition)

source_text: au bout du fossé, la culbute
english_translation: danger is imminent
Cultural_Context: (lit.: at the end of a ditch, a somersault)

source_text: au royaume des aveugles, les borgnes sont rois
english_translation: in the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed man is king
Cultural_Context: (lit.: in the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed are kings)

source_text: aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait
english_translation: said and done
Cultural_Context: (lit.: soon said, soon done)

source_text: autant des têtes, autant d’avis
english_translation: too many cooks spoil the broth
Cultural_Context: (lit.: so many heads, so much advice)

source_text: autant en emporte le vent
english_translation: empty promises
Cultural_Context: (lit.: as much as the wind can carry)

source_text: autres temps, autres mœurs
english_translation: times change
Cultural_Context: (lit.: other times, other customs)

source_text: aux grands maux, les grands remèdes
english_translation: big problems require big solutions; desperate situations call for desperate measures
Cultural_Context: (lit.: for large evils, great remedies)

source_text: aux innocents les mains pleines
english_translation: fortune favors the innocent
Cultural_Context: (lit.: the innocent have their hands full)

source_text: avant de balayer devant la porte du voisin, il faut commencer par balayer devant sa propre porte
english_translation: before cleaning up your neighbor’s door, you must start by cleaning your own
Cultural_Context: (lit.: before sweeping at your neighbor's door, you must sweep your own door)

source_text: avec des “si,” on mettrait Paris en bouteille
english_translation: if ifs and ands were pots and pans, there’d be no work for tinker’s hands; if wishes were horses
Cultural_Context: (lit.: with ifs, Paris could be put in a bottle)

source_text: avoir le beurre et l’argent du beurre
english_translation: have one’s cake and eat it too
Cultural_Context: (lit.: to have one’s butter and the money for it)

source_text: L’argent ne se trouve pas sous le sabot d'un cheval
english_translation: Money doesn't grow on trees
Cultural_Context: Money must be earned through work, not easily found.

source_text: Le monde appartient à ceux qui se lèvent tôt
english_translation: The early bird catches the worm
Cultural_Context: Success comes to those who are diligent and start early.

source_text: Deux avis valent mieux qu'un
english_translation: Two heads are better than one
Cultural_Context: Two opinions are worth more than one.

source_text: À mauvais ouvrier, mauvais outils
english_translation: A bad workman quarrels with his tools
Cultural_Context: To a bad workman, bad tools.

source_text: Faire d'une pierre, deux coups
english_translation: To kill two birds with one stone
Cultural_Context: To make from one stone, two strikes.

source_text: 'Impossible' n'est pas français
english_translation: There is no such word as 'can't.'
Cultural_Context: 'Impossible' is not French.

source_text: Deux s'amusent, trois s'ennuient
english_translation: Two is company, three is a crowd
Cultural_Context: Two have fun, three get bored.

source_text: Qui se ressemble, s'assemble
english_translation: Birds of a feather flock together
Cultural_Context: Those who are similar, gather together.

source_text: Vouloir, c'est pouvoir
english_translation: Where there's a will there's a way
Cultural_Context: To want is to be able.

source_text: Ce ne sont pas les mots qui comptent mais les actions
english_translation: Actions speak louder than words
Cultural_Context: It is not the words that count but the actions.

source_text: À beaucoup d'ouvriers la tâche est aisée
english_translation: Many hands make light work
Cultural_Context: To lots of workers the task is easy.

source_text: Bouillon de chou fait perdre au médecin cinq sous
english_translation: An apple a day keeps the doctor away
Cultural_Context: Cabbage soup costs the doctor five pennies.

source_text: La beauté est affaire de goût
english_translation: Beauty is in the eyes of the beholder
Cultural_Context: Beauty is a matter of taste.

source_text: Ce n'est pas la mer à boire!
english_translation: It's not that bad / hard / difficult! It's not such a big deal!
Cultural_Context: It's not the sea that you have to drink!

source_text: C'est mon petit doigt qui me le dit
english_translation: A little bird tells me
Cultural_Context: It's my little finger that tells me.

source_text: Quand le vin est tiré, il faut le boire
english_translation: There's no going back. You have to see it through.
Cultural_Context: Once the wine has been fetched, you have to drink it.

source_text: Il n’y a que les imbéciles qui ne changent pas d’avis
english_translation: Only fools never change their minds
Cultural_Context: Our opinions may vary, and people clinging to their beliefs or decisions when they have every reason not to are being stupid. We use this proverb to point out stubbornness or to justify changing our minds.

source_text: On n’apprend pas au vieux singe à faire la grimace
english_translation: This old dog knows all the tricks
Cultural_Context: You don’t need to teach something to someone who has much more experience than you have. We typically use this expression when someone with less experience or knowledge is trying to explain something we find obvious or easy.

source_text: Il n’y a que la vérité qui blesse
english_translation: Truth hurts
Cultural_Context: If you feel offended by a statement or reproach, it only proves that it was true. The most hurtful comments are the ones we deserve. This expression is often used as a taunt, or when someone is denying their fault or wrongdoing and acting offended by the accusation.

source_text: La vengeance est un plat qui se mange froid
english_translation: Revenge is a dish best served cold
Cultural_Context: Vengeance is more satisfying when delayed and exacted with a clear head. You’ll take more pleasure if you wait until the heat of anger has cooled off, rather than take revenge as an immediate act of rage.

source_text: À vaincre sans péril, on triomphe sans gloire
english_translation: No guts, no glory
Cultural_Context: Success won’t come if you’re not brave enough to take risks. This is a quote from Le Cid.

source_text: Il ne faut pas mettre la charrue avant les bœufs
english_translation: Don’t put the cart before the horse
Cultural_Context: This expression from the fifteenth century means that you shouldn’t go so fast that you fail to do things in the right order.

source_text: On n’est jamais mieux servi que par soi-même
english_translation: If you want something done right, do it yourself
Cultural_Context: If you want something done exactly the way you want it, you should just do it yourself.

source_text: Qui ne risque rien n’a rien
english_translation: Nothing ventured, nothing gained
Cultural_Context: One must take risks to achieve something. If you don’t risk anything, you won’t get anything good.

source_text: Ne remets pas à demain ce que tu peux faire aujourd’hui
english_translation: Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do today
Cultural_Context: No time like the present! You shouldn’t delay doing something if you can do it right now.

source_text: Les chiens ne font pas des chats
english_translation: The apple doesn’t fall far from the tree
Cultural_Context: Children usually have similar characteristics or qualities to those of their parents.

source_text: Rien ne sert de courir, il faut partir à point
english_translation: Slow and steady wins the race
Cultural_Context: (from La Fontaine’s fable Le Lièvre et la Tortue)

source_text: Chassez le naturel, il revient au galop
english_translation: A leopard cannot change its spots
Cultural_Context: If you go against your nature, it will never last.

source_text: Il n’est pire aveugle que celui qui ne veut pas voir
english_translation: You cannot reason with someone who’s not interested in the truth
Cultural_Context: (variant of “There are none so blind as those who will not see”)

source_text: On ne fait pas d’omelette sans casser d’oeufs
english_translation: No pain no gain
Cultural_Context: You cannot achieve great things without making sacrifices.

source_text: Les petits ruisseaux font les grandes rivières
english_translation: Little streams make great rivers
Cultural_Context: This proverb emphasizes that small efforts or contributions can accumulate into something much larger over time. It is often used to encourage consistency and patience in achieving goals.

source_text: Ce qui est fait n’est plus à faire
english_translation: What is done is no longer to be done
Cultural_Context: This simply means that once a task is completed, there’s no need to do it again. Often used to underline that you should complete tasks properly the first time.

source_text: L’appétit vient en mangeant
english_translation: Appetite comes while eating
Cultural_Context: This suggests that the more you have of something, the more you want. It can refer to food literally, but it’s also used figuratively to highlight how taking the first step can increase motivation.

source_text: Il faut réfléchir avant d’agir
english_translation: One must think before acting
Cultural_Context: A straightforward exhortation to consider consequences before taking action. Similar to “Look before you leap.”

source_text: Un malheur ne vient jamais seul
english_translation: A misfortune never arrives alone
Cultural_Context: This proverb reflects the belief that bad events tend to happen in clusters (“When it rains, it pours”).

source_text: Qui va à la chasse perd sa place
english_translation: He who goes hunting loses his seat
Cultural_Context: Commonly used when someone leaves their seat or position temporarily and finds it taken upon return. “You snooze, you lose.”

source_text: Tel père, tel fils
english_translation: Like father, like son
Cultural_Context: This emphasizes that children often resemble their parents in character, behavior, or fate.

source_text: Loin des yeux, loin du cœur
english_translation: Far from the eyes, far from the heart
Cultural_Context: Suggests that if someone or something is not physically present, it can be easily forgotten.

source_text: Mieux vaut tard que jamais
english_translation: Better late than never
Cultural_Context: Encourages taking action or completing a task even if it’s delayed, rather than abandoning it altogether.

source_text: La fin justifie les moyens
english_translation: The end justifies the means
Cultural_Context: This can be used either positively or critically to say that achieving a goal can sometimes excuse the methods used.

source_text: Qui veut voyager loin ménage sa monture
english_translation: He who wants to travel far spares his mount
Cultural_Context: Encourages pacing oneself and preserving one’s resources to achieve long-term objectives.

source_text: À l’impossible nul n’est tenu
english_translation: No one is bound to do the impossible
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that no one can be expected to accomplish the unachievable.

source_text: Quand on parle du loup, on en voit la queue
english_translation: When one speaks of the wolf, you see its tail
Cultural_Context: The French counterpart to “Speak of the devil and he appears.” It’s often said when the subject of a conversation suddenly appears.

source_text: Un ‘tiens’ vaut mieux que deux ‘tu l’auras’
english_translation: One “here you go” is better than two “you’ll get it”
Cultural_Context: Similar to “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush,” it emphasizes that a guaranteed or immediate gain is more valuable than a larger but uncertain promise.

source_text: A beau mentir qui vient de loin
english_translation: He who comes from afar can easily lie
Cultural_Context: Suggests that someone whose story cannot be easily verified can make grand or false claims without fear of being exposed.

source_text: L’argent est la racine de tous les maux
english_translation: Money is the root of all evil
Cultural_Context: Classic warning about the dangers of greed and how money can corrupt.

source_text: Nécessité est mère d’invention
english_translation: Necessity is the mother of invention
Cultural_Context: When you really need something, you find a way to make it happen.

source_text: Rira bien qui rira le dernier
english_translation: He who laughs last laughs longest
Cultural_Context: The person who has the last laugh is the one who ultimately succeeds.

source_text: Une minute d’hésitation peut coûter cher
english_translation: He who hesitates is lost
Cultural_Context: A moment of doubt can lead to missing a great opportunity.

source_text: C’est dans le besoin que l’on connaît ses vrais amis
english_translation: A friend in need is a friend indeed
Cultural_Context: True friends reveal themselves when times are hard.

source_text: Nécessité fait loi
english_translation: Beggars can’t be choosers
Cultural_Context: When you have no choice, you must accept what is offered.

source_text: Rira vendredi dimanche pleurera
english_translation: He who laughs on Friday will cry on Sunday
Cultural_Context: What starts well may end badly — don’t get too cocky too soon.

source_text: Chaque chose en son temps
english_translation: Don’t cross your bridges before you come to them
Cultural_Context: Do things in the proper order; don’t rush ahead.

source_text: Un petit service en vaut un autre
english_translation: You scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours
Cultural_Context: One good turn deserves another.

source_text: Un point à temps en vaut cent
english_translation: A stitch in time saves nine
Cultural_Context: Fixing a small problem early saves much bigger trouble later.

source_text: L’argent ne fait pas le bonheur
english_translation: Money cannot buy happiness
Cultural_Context: Nearly identical to its English counterpart, this expression means that although money lets you buy things, it’s not enough to achieve happiness. The most materialistic people often follow it with mais il y contribue (“but it contributes to it”).

source_text: Il ne faut pas vendre la peau de l’ours avant de l’avoir tué
english_translation: Don’t count your chickens before they hatch
Cultural_Context: This traditional saying comes from Old French. It means that you should wait to act until you know that something is certain.

source_text: Chat échaudé craint l’eau froide
english_translation: Once bitten, twice shy
Cultural_Context: This is what you’d say if you were scared of doing something again because you previously had an unpleasant experience doing that thing. Bad experiences make us cautious.

source_text: On ne change pas une équipe qui gagne
english_translation: If it ain’t broken, don’t fix it
Cultural_Context: There’s no need to make any changes to something that’s already working well.

source_text: Il vaut mieux prévenir que guérir
english_translation: Better safe than sorry
Cultural_Context: You might use this proverb when it seems wiser to be careful and protect yourself instead of taking unnecessary risks.

source_text: Il n’y a pas de fumée sans feu
english_translation: Where there is smoke, there is fire
Cultural_Context: If there’s any sign of something being true, then it must be at least partly true.

source_text: Qui aime bien châtie bien
english_translation: Spare the rod and spoil the child
Cultural_Context: When you love someone, you’ll punish them proportionally to their wrongdoing instead of being too harsh or ignoring their fault.

source_text: Paris ne s’est pas fait en un jour
english_translation: Paris wasn’t built in a day
Cultural_Context: Just like the English saying “Rome wasn’t built in a day,” it reminds us that significant achievements require time and effort. It’s a call for patience and perseverance.

source_text: Qui vole un œuf vole un bœuf
english_translation: He who steals an egg will steal an ox
Cultural_Context: It warns that small misdeeds can lead to bigger crimes or that a dishonest person might not stop at minor offenses.

source_text: Un clou chasse l'autre
english_translation: One nail drives out another
Cultural_Context: Life goes on.

source_text: En tout pays, il y a une lieue de mauvais chemin
english_translation: In every country there is a league/area of bad road
Cultural_Context: There will be bumps in the smoothest roads.

source_text: Tout vient à point à qui sait attendre
english_translation: All comes on time to the one who knows how to wait
Cultural_Context: All things come to those who wait.

source_text: Il n’y a pas plus sourd que celui qui ne veut pas entendre
english_translation: The deafest are those who don’t want to listen
Cultural_Context: Stubborn teenagers might hear this French proverb quite often, especially if they’re not heeding their parents’ advice.

source_text: Ce n’est pas la mer à boire
english_translation: It’s not the end of the world
Cultural_Context: If you’re exasperated by someone who complains, and complains, and complains some more, simply for the sake of complaining (and their life is pretty easy and carefree) you can say to them: Stop complaining. It’s not the end of the world.

source_text: À bon chat, bon rat
english_translation: To a good cat, a good rat
Cultural_Context: Tit for tat./Equally matched./To meet your match

source_text: Il faut tourner sept fois sa langue dans sa bouche avant de parler
english_translation: You should turn your tongue around in your mouth seven times before you speak
Cultural_Context: Think before you speak

source_text: Ce n’est pas à un vieux singe qu’on apprend à faire des grimaces
english_translation: You don’t teach an old monkey how to make funny faces
Cultural_Context: I wasn’t born yesterday

source_text: Impossible n’est pas français
english_translation: Impossible isn’t French
Cultural_Context: There’s no such thing as “impossible”

source_text: Bien mal acquis ne profite jamais
english_translation: Goods badly acquired never benefit
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to admonish someone, like a wayward child who steals, emphasizing that ill-gotten gains do not benefit and carry wider implications, staying with them for life.

source_text: Qui vole un oeuf vole un boeuf
english_translation: Who steals an egg steals a cow
Cultural_Context: This 19th Century proverb communicates that theft is theft regardless of scale, and stealing small things leads to stealing bigger ones, with punishment being equally harsh in the era it originated.

source_text: Les jours se suivent et ne se ressemblent pas
english_translation: The days follow one another and do not resemble each other
Cultural_Context: This saying, with origins unknown but noted as originating in a different language, highlights how consecutive days can vary greatly.

source_text: C'est pas demain la veille!
english_translation: It's not the day before tomorrow!
Cultural_Context: This short proverb about life is roughly similar to 'Don't put the cart before the horse'.

source_text: On ne peut pas plaire à tout le monde
english_translation: We can't please everyone

source_text: Tall oaks from little acorns grow
english_translation: Tall oaks from little acorns grow

source_text: Vouloir c'est pouvoir
english_translation: Where there's a will, there's a way

source_text: Tant qu'il y a de la vie, il y a de l'espoir
english_translation: While there is life, there is hope

source_text: Les grands esprits se rencontrent
english_translation: Great minds think alike

source_text: Même les meilleures choses ont une fin
english_translation: Even the best things come to an end

source_text: Bon à tout, bon à rien
english_translation: Jack of all trades, master of none
